content: The windsock pattern or windsock lesion is a diagnostic feature associated with left ventricular outflow tract aneurysms. This pattern is typically identified through echocardiography, where the mitral valve and left atrium are seen extending into the left ventricular outflow tract. Pathomorphological images provide further insights into the sinus of Valsalva aneurysms. These include gross anatomical depictions of aneurysms, such as a windsock-like opening beneath the anterior leaflet of the tricuspid valve extending into the right ventricle. Other images show aneurysms with ruptured aortic cusps due to infective endocarditis, as well as infected aneurysms with extensive ulceration and fibrinous material caused by Staphylococcus infection of a bicuspid valve. In some cases, ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysms are visualized grossly, with natural color images showing hemorrhagic lesions in the left coronary sinus or aneurysms pointing into the left atrium through the mitral ring at the anterior mitral commissure. Close-up views of the aortic valve may reveal aneurysms in the non-coronary cusp, with or without the use of a probe for orientation. Additional cases document ruptures below the tricuspid ring, sometimes associated with a patent foramen ovale. Infected aneurysms may exhibit fibrin exudate and valve scarring, requiring careful examination to identify lesions caused by pathogens like Staphylococcus. The literature provides extensive documentation of sinus of Valsalva aneurysms, including their anatomy, classification, and clinical presentations. Studies have explored congenital aneurysms, traumatic fistulas, and complications such as bacterial endocarditis or fungal infections like Aspergillus. Surgical repair outcomes, particularly for ruptured aneurysms, have been evaluated, with long-term follow-up data available. Diagnostic techniques such as echocardiography, transesophageal imaging, and magnetic resonance imaging have been instrumental in identifying these lesions preoperatively.
